data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible as a non-inductive 'critical preference' based on informational content: we prefer the theory that has survived the most severe tests because it possesses the highest empirical content and thus offers the greatest opportunity for future falsification, not because it is likely true.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If scientists prefer a low-content, tautological theory that has survived many trivial tests over a high-content theory that has survived fewer severe tests.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severity' of a test implicitly relies on inductive assumptions about the stability of nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent cannot distinguish between a theory surviving due to luck versus surviving due to its structural robustness without invoking induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Informational Utility Maximization: The agent selects the hypothesis with the highest remaining falsifiability (boldness) that has not yet been falsified. Survival is merely the condition that allows the high-content theory to remain in the game; the preference is for the content itself, which is logically distinct from probability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
